source.title: RealSyn: An Effective and Scalable Multimodal Interleaved Document Transformation Paradigm
source.authors: Tian-Cheng Gu; Kai-Cheng Yang; Chaoyi Zhang; Yin Xie; Xiang An; Zi-Yong Feng; Dongnan Liu; Wei-Dong Cai; Jian-Kang Deng

record.file_problem: The full paper and supplementary material are present. Some table layouts are flattened, but the reported averages and scaling equations are legible.
record.tranche_reason: The paper tests downstream performance scaling for vision-language models, a different modality and setting from language-model pretraining-loss scaling.
record.gate_note: The paper does not measure held-out language-model cross-entropy, language-model parameter/token/compute scaling, or compute-optimal allocation. Its own relevant results are CLIP downstream-performance results as data or model scale changes, including fitted data-scaling curves. Other dataset comparisons and ablations are not scaling-law measurements; claims cited from other work are not recorded as results.
record.test_reason: The paper trains CLIP models (vision-language contrastive) at several data scales and fits downstream accuracy against sample count, then extrapolates from 12M–60M to 100M. It also reports downstream accuracy across three ViT sizes at 30M. This bears on V6 (downstream predictability with scale) in a new setting. It reports no pretraining loss, so V1–V5 and V7 are not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that RealSyn gives state-of-the-art CLIP downstream performance at matched scales and 'demonstrates robust scalability.' They also claim it shows steeper model-scaling curves than LAION, and that their fitted inverse-log data scaling law predicts the 100M trend and suggests a ViT-B/32 performance ceiling.
record.recipe_differences: This is a vision-language contrastive-learning study using downstream metrics and data/model scale comparisons. It does not use the language-model held-out-loss measurement, parameter/token/compute sweeps, or compute-optimal allocation procedure of the original scaling-law studies.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported performance varies with training-data source and scale and with model size. The scaling analysis fits inverse-logarithmic functions on RealSyn data for ViT-B/32; the paper does not compare fitting procedures.

fits_no_version.finding: Downstream CLIP accuracy vs data scale is fit by an inverse-logarithmic function with finite asymptotes (0.80 linear probe, 0.62 zero-shot, 0.56 robustness). The authors read these as an upper bound for ViT-B/32.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Downstream accuracy of fixed-size vision-language models saturates toward a model-specific ceiling as data grows, following a non-power-law (inverse-log) form.

record.problems: The scaling evidence is for CLIP downstream metrics, not held-out pretraining loss. The extrapolation is reported as trend validation without numerical prediction errors or uncertainty estimates; model-scaling curve values are only available in a figure.
record.rows_left_out: Single-scale downstream dataset comparisons, captioning results, and text/sampling ablations were left out because they do not report a scale-prediction result. The qualitative model-scaling results are retained in R13–R15.

untested.parts: No held-out pretraining loss and no LM parameter/token/compute sweep.
No loss extrapolation. Only downstream-accuracy extrapolation (12–60M to 100M), recorded under V6.
No shape comparison at fixed parameter count.
No pretraining (contrastive) loss reported as a function of scale, so the power-law loss form in vision-language is not tested.
Predictability from pretraining loss is not tested. Model-size scaling has only three sizes and no fitted law.
No comparison of fitting choices or exponents across setups.

missing.what: Across-scale trajectories of downstream averages (15M→30M→100M) for RealSyn and for LAION. These are the actual data-scaling evidence; the current R1–R9 encode only fixed-scale dataset contrasts.
Numeric model-scaling results for ViT-B/32, B/16 and L/14 at 30M on both datasets. R13–R15 mark these as figure-only, but the tables give them.
Intermediate data-scale points (12M–60M) used for the fit, and a numerical prediction error at 100M.

record.verdict_notes: The study is primarily a dataset paper. Scaling evidence is secondary and concerns downstream accuracy of CLIP, not LM loss; it is treated as T3 bearing on V6 only. The fit is inverse-log, not power-law, and cites Kaplan et al. only as inspiration. Training epochs are fixed at 32, so compute grows with data. Parameter counts are not stated. The 100M check is my own computation from Eq.3 assuming natural log; the paper reports no error.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out language-model pretraining loss or language-model parameter, token, or compute sweep.
No tests of small-run language-model loss fits predicting much larger runs.
No fixed-compute allocation sweep or comparison of parameter and token growth.
No comparison of architecture shapes at a fixed parameter count.
The paper studies vision-language models, but does not test whether the same power-law form holds for held-out pretraining loss in other modalities or regimes.
Tests downstream CLIP performance against data and model scale, not downstream performance against language-model pretraining loss.
No comparison of fitting choices or exponents, compute-optimal splits, or evidence that scaling curves bend away from a single power law.

relationships.condition: CLIP ViT-B/32 on RealSyn, downstream averages vs training samples, fit on 12M–60M and extrapolated to 100M
relationships.reason: Authors fit inverse-log laws and say they predict the 100M results. Eq.3 reproduces the Table 1/2/4 100M values within about 1 point (R10–R12). No error is reported, and the curve form is a saturating inverse-log, not a power law.
relationships.display_finding: Saturating inverse-log fits extrapolated from 12M–60M samples reproduced the 100M-sample downstream averages within about 1 point.

relationships.condition: CLIP ViT-B/32, B/16, L/14 trained on RealSyn30M or LAION30M
relationships.reason: Downstream averages rise monotonically with model size on all three metrics for both datasets (Tables 9–11; R13–R15). There are only three sizes and no fitted law, so the support is for improvement with scale, not for predictability.
relationships.display_finding: All three downstream averages increased monotonically across three model sizes on both datasets, without a fitted predictive relationship.
